title: A local governor is founded and seated at Qurṭuba, the old seat of the caliphs, to carry the crown's authority up and down the great river through the lands won in 1349
The amir marries his Marīnid bride, Duʿāʾ, fulfilling the betrothal agreed with the house of Fās in January 1348
The amir marries his Ḥafṣid bride, Tizemt, fulfilling the betrothal agreed with Tūnis in July 1345: his third wife, and his second bride from the Maghrib in three months

The Ghana betrothal is fulfilled, though not as the court intended: Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, the amir's elder brother and lately his regent, marries Fatiu, daughter of the old ruler of Ghana, and goes south across the desert to live in her land
source: Trent's account (the exact date isn't given; reported by 19 November 1355)

title: With Faraj gone south, his seat in the dīwān goes to Yaḥyā Raḥḥū, the Zenata general who led the Volunteers of the Faith against Arghūn and the three crowns

The Powerful Harem: as the harem grows with the amir's Marīnid and Ḥafṣid brides, it becomes an institution of the crown. The amir is no puppet of it, but cunning concubines flood the court and draw power inward around the throne, to the nobles' chagrin; women may now sit in the dīwān

title: Yaḥyā Raḥḥū dies of an illness, aged 54, only lately seated in the dīwān. The court calls it a coincidence
source: Trent's account (late 1355; the exact day isn't given)

title: Duʿāʾ, the Marīnid wife and the most capable of the amir's wives, takes the empty seat in the dīwān: the first woman of the harem to sit in the council
